AJK.name: Juneau
AJK.excerpt: By the weekend, powerful swell from distant storms will continue to impact our coast; however, winds and fresh seas should be trending down. Look for our next large low to move into the Gulf by Monday or Tuesday of next week.

sections.name: Evening, Aviation, And Long Term Forecast Updates
paragraphs: A strong front continues to push through the panhandle this evening, with wind advisories remaining in effect across the southern panhandle and reported gusts 40 to 45 mph at Hydaburg, Metlakatla, Klawock and Ketchikan. New this evening is the issuance of short duration wind advisory through early Tuesday morning for the Downtown Juneau, Douglas, and Thane areas as a mountain wave wind event is ongoing. This is a localized strong wind with reported NE- ly gusts at the AML Dock and AJ Dock up to 45 mph, up to 40 mph at the Marine Exchange, while winds near the Juneau Airport are near calm. Likely seeing the peak strength of these winds now for the downtown area with the strongest E/W gradient diminishing after midnight through 3am Tuesday morning.

In addition, upgraded Northern Lynn Canal to a Gale Warning with winds steadily increasing through the evening as the front pushes northward. Anticipating steady sustained 35 to 40 kt northerly winds with gusts up to 50 kts continuing into late tonight before diminishing slightly through Tuesday morning. However marine winds increase once more into Tuesday afternoon as another front pushes into the southern panhandle and northward through Tuesday evening.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: /Thursday through Sunday/... Thursdays weather maker is currently an impressive hurricane force extratropical cyclone located near 44N 175W. This system will continue to travel east through the next few days but weaken as it moves into the Gulf, with the low center west of Dixon Entrance by Thursday morning. Overall confidence is high in the location of this system, with a wide range of pressure depth solutions; currently thinking the low will reach near 985mb by Thursday morning. As this system lifts north along the Alexander Archipelago coast expect outflow winds to start to diminish thru the Inner Channels, with another round of precipitation into Saturday morning. Currently not expecting any widespread snow impacts at sea level, warm air should have successfully infiltrated most areas across the Panhandle with the exception of Haines and Skagway highways. Look for a break in precipitation Sunday.

By the weekend, powerful swell from distant storms will continue to impact our coast; however, winds and fresh seas should be trending down. Look for our next large low to move into the Gulf by Monday or Tuesday of next week.

sections.name: Prev Discussion
paragraphs: ...ISSUED AT 407 PM AKST Mon Nov 23 2026...
- Incoming front will bring breezy conditions to the southern panhandle with wind advisories issued through 3 PM tomorrow.
- Possibility for mixing rain and snow in the central panhandle up to Icy Strait corridor including Juneau. No accumulation is expected.
- Multiple rounds of rain and wind are likely this week with the possibility of some drier and cooler weather this weekend.

SHORT TERM.../Through Tuesday night/...A large system in the Pacific brings the first of multiple fronts across the panhandle tonight through the morning. As of 3 PM AKST, this front has already pushed into the southernmost part of the panhandle, bringing rain and gusty winds. As the main low remains far south of the panhandle, ahead of this front will be northerly and northeasterly winds picking up tonight. With this, some locations will be seeing some downsloping gusty winds, such as downtown Juneau and South Douglas keeping temperatures warmer at sea level compared to locations with calm winds. This means that while many areas across the northern panhandle will see cold temperatures 30 degrees or less last before the cloud cover moves in, localized areas experiencing downsloping winds will see temperatures into the mid 30s to around 40 this evening.

As the front pushes northward overnight, areas south of Frederick Sound and along the central outer coastline will see rain, with gusty easterly winds. Prince of Wales Island, Annette Island, and Ketchikan will see some 15 to 25 mph winds with gusts up to 45 mph tonight with this front. As it travels northward, this front will begin to shear apart and weaken, becoming less widespread with precipitation and with less moisture making it into the northern panhandle. The area with the lowest confidence on seeing much if any precipitation is the far northern panhandle by Haines and Skagway, as well as Yakutat, with this front shearing westward and likely not even making it into Yakutat at all. Skagway and Haines will see lower chances of precipitation, but any that falls will be very light snow with little accumulation of 0.5 inches or less overnight into tomorrow. Juneau and other locations around Icy Strait corridor are expected to stay cold enough to see a chance of snow, with more likely a rain and snow mix overnight than fully snow, though the concerns on how much precipitation will make it to the area and how dry it will be near the surface brings a lot of uncertainty into the forecast for tonight. The confidence is higher for a rain and snow mix overnight into the morning, with little to no accumulation at sea level, however QPF amounts and precipitation type may be very localized.

After this front will be another, generally warmer and slightly stronger, front moving in Tuesday morning through the day. It is similar to the first in how it moves into the area, however it looks to keep moisture pushing further northward than this initial front. This will bring some more precipitation into the northern panhandle, however the chances for snow diminish with this warmer air pushing in.

The first of several gale force fronts are working their way into the southern panhandle and moving northward this evening. Strong gale force easterlies will gradually weaken as they move northward, stalling offshore of Cross Sound due to stronger, denser northerly winds out of interior passes. As winds shift from easterly to southeasterly behind the front, wave heights between 15-20 ft will build in the eastern gulf. The second front, again an easterly front, looks to develop off of a closed low off the coast of Prince of Wales Island. There is some uncertainty regarding the location of this low, with a majority of solutions leaning towards more than 80 NM offshore vs a minority of models of 20 NM offshore. Both will be at least gale force, with the stronger, closer closed low generating possibly storm force southerly gusts on the southeast flank.

Strong northerlies out of interior passes continue to build, with the highlight being Taku Inlet and Lynn Canal down to point Couverden. Point Couverden continues to be a headache, with sustained winds hovering around near gale to gale force from a tip jet set up. Down south, shifting winds from more northeasterly to southeasterly will follow the front, staying around that 25-30 knot range during the shift. Highest uncertainty is how far north the southeasterlies will reach on this initial front. Stephens Passage near Five Finger in particular does have a chance to tip southerly with this front briefly before shifting back northerly for the next front Tuesday.

BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: A weak system will move into the area on Thursday, bringing valley rain and mountain snow. Precipitation amounts with this system will be light. A cold front will graze the region on Friday bringing moderate snows to the mountains into Saturday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Light valley rain and mountain snow showers expected through this afternoon.
- Dry conditions on Tuesday with valley fog developing overnight.
- Unsettled weather will return Wednesday through the end of the week alongside warmer temps and higher snow levels.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: A shortwave ridge will transition over the area tonight and Tuesday, with partial clearing and patchy fog developing overnight. Southwest flow aloft ahead of an approaching system will shift the surface winds to E-SE over the higher terrain. This will push low clouds and stratus toward the Lower Treasure Valley into Baker County, along the I-84 corridor. Slight improvement in fog and stratus on Tuesday afternoon in these areas. The system will weaken as it moves inland bringing increased clouds and showers late Tuesday into Wednesday morning. Showers will mainly be confined to eastern OR, and the west central ID mountains on Wednesday morning before tapering off during the afternoon.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: A weak system will move into the area on Thursday, bringing valley rain and mountain snow. Precipitation amounts with this system will be light. A cold front will graze the region on Friday bringing moderate snows to the mountains into Saturday. Current forecast does not reflect this system. Upper level ridging returns for Sunday and Monday with fog and low stratus possible in the valleys.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: Temperatures and precip chances will remain highly uncertain for the weekend and into Monday. 25th to 75th percentile highs differ by around 10 to 15 degrees across the plains during this time.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - A gradual warming trend likely through the rest of the week, with quiet weather expected through Thanksgiving
- Next storm system could bring some snow to the central and northern mountains Friday into Saturday.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Isolated light snow showers will continue overnight for the higher terrain, with precip chances ending by early tomorrow morning as the upper level shortwave and jet continue moving off to the east. We're already seeing some patchy fog develop along the CO/WY border late this evening. Patchy fog could spread further south and west overnight, potentially impacting the northern I-25 corridor. But fog is expected to stay north of the metro.

Quiet weather is expected for much of this week. The upper level trough, which moved over the area today, will sit to our east for the next couple of days. Another trough will develop over the West Coast by early Wednesday. In between these two systems, we'll have weak ridging aloft over/just west of the area. Temperatures will gradually warm through the work week, with highs reaching near 60 for much of the plains by Friday. Thanksgiving looks rather pleasant weather-wise, with highs in the 50s across the plains and partly cloudy skies. Mid and upper level northwest winds will strengthen on Friday, bringing moisture into the area. Models vary with the depth of the upper level shortwave and the placement of the upper level jet. Some runs have a broader longwave trough with the jet more to our north, putting us in the right exit region. While other runs, have a more potent shortwave and put us in the left exit region of the jet. The latter would be much more favorable for precip and cooler temperatures in our area, with the most likely timing of precip sometime late Friday through early Sunday. Looking at cluster analysis, about 55% of the ensemble members in the LREF bring a deeper shortwave with light rain making it off the higher terrain and into the plains on Saturday, with 19% of the ensemble members bringing snow onto the plains.

Temperatures and precip chances will remain highly uncertain for the weekend and into Monday. 25th to 75th percentile highs differ by around 10 to 15 degrees across the plains during this time. Precipitation chances will depend heavily on what happens with this first system mentioned above and a potential second shortwave Monday.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Monday...A fast moving shortwave trough aloft will sweep eastward across our counties, and with adequate mid level moisture, will produce orographic snows for our Snowy and Sierra Madre Ranges.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Elevated winds are possible Tuesday afternoon through the night for the wind prone areas of southeast Wyoming.
- Another round of even stronger winds and more widespread is possible Thursday into Friday.
- Significant forecast uncertainty exists for the weekend due to an unusually large range of possible forecast outcomes.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Very chilly day across the region as low clouds have remained mostly socked in, keeping temperatures around or below freezing. The exceptions to this have been along the I-80 corridor from Arlington through Cheyenne where breaks in the clouds have allowed for some sunshine, and temperatures have jumped into the mid to upper 30's. Aloft, a trough is passing across the Rockies with the strongest and most impactful portion of this feature well to our south in the southern Four Corners area. Because of this with the best instability and moisture to our south, the majority of this feature will not produce any noteworthy precipitation activity outside of some very light snow in the mountains.

Moving into Tuesday, we'll become enveloped in split flow aloft as the troughing to the south begins to deepen as it moves into the Central US while a new low over Canada dives down into the Dakotas. Under this pattern, we'll see pressure gradients tighten with an elongated jet feature develop and stretch over the US. While the strongest portions of this jet will be associated with the respective features creating it, we'll still see our region under a stronger northerly flow aloft that will fuel enhanced surface winds for the day. In house guidance still isn't excited enough that we should see High Wind Warning level criteria with probabilities only maxing around 40% for the Arlington area at the highest, but stronger gusts of around 40-55 mph are possible with an errant gust or two nearing that threshold of 58+ mph. Otherwise it'll be a dry day with no precipitation expected as highs recover east of the Laramie Range, increasing by around 10 degrees. Some morning fog could still linger for areas of Converse, Niobrara, Platte, and Goshen Counties, but increasing winds and drier air should help to alleviate this by later Tuesday morning.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Wednesday...Ridging aloft will keep it dry with relatively light winds. 700 mb temperatures near 1 Celsius will yield high temperatures in the 40s.

Thanksgiving...The next shortwave trough aloft moves from eastern Montana and eastern Wyoming in the morning, to the western high plains by evening. This system is moisture starved with only perhaps some mid and high level cloudiness. Low and mid level gradients suggest a breezy to windy day. More mild downwind of the Laramie Range and I-25 due to downslope warming. Continued cold to the west of I-25.

Friday...Looks like the beginning of a windy weekend with strong northwest flow aloft and deep unidirectional flow in the atmosphere. Will likely see high winds for our typically wind prone locations such as Arlington, Bordeaux and the I-80 Summit, with strong winds possibly in nearby locations of southeast Wyoming as well. Enough low and mid level moisture for orographic snows across the Snowy and Sierra Madre Ranges. Despite the winds, it will remain relatively mild with 700 mb temperatures near -4 Celsius yielding high temperatures in the 40s west of I-25, with low to mid 50s east of I- 25.

Saturday...Strong west northwest flow will occur in the low and mid levels, and looking like a more widespread high wind event for much of southeast Wyoming and parts of the Nebraska Panhandle. Again, looks like adequate mid level moisture for orographic snows across the northern Laramie, Snowy and Sierra Madre Ranges. Will see a slow cooling trend over the weekend based on 700 mb temperatures.

Sunday...The flow aloft turns westerly though still remains strong enough at low and mid levels for windy conditions across the wind prone locations. A surface high across the central Plains states will slide across our eastern counties, to the east of I-25, with winds lessening.

Monday...A fast moving shortwave trough aloft will sweep eastward across our counties, and with adequate mid level moisture, will produce orographic snows for our Snowy and Sierra Madre Ranges. Temperatures similar to Sunday, in the 40s west of I-25, with upper 40s to mid 50s further east.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: After this ridge moves through, deterministic guidance is coming into better agreement that flow starts to split by Thursday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Snow comes to an end bringing clear and dry conditions for Tuesday and Wednesday
- Active weather remains possible late Thanksgiving week, but some details still remain uncertain. Stay tuned for updates to timing and impacts as they become available.

sections.name: Update
paragraphs: Snow has come to an end across the central and southern mountains this evening, with little in the way of additional impacts expected. As a result, all of the Winter Weather Advisories have been dropped.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: CALM AND DRY CONDITIONS EXPECTED TUESDAY AND WEDNESDAY

Snow showers are coming to an end over the central and southern mountains. Skies will clear while fog begins to develop in mountain valleys. A fast moving ridge will develop in the wake of this system. Clear and dry conditions are expected for Tuesday and Wednesday as this ridge moves over the region.
ANOTHER ROUND OF SNOW EXPECTED AFTER THANKSGIVING

After this ridge moves through, deterministic guidance is coming into better agreement that flow starts to split by Thursday. A ridge begins developing over SoCal which will bring a cutoff low to our south while another powerful system moves to our north and east. A continuation of dry conditions with above normal temperatures is expected for Thanksgiving as both systems move away from our CWA. By Friday, the SoCal ridge breaks down and another system approaches our area. Flow turns northwesterly and with it, there's an increased chance of snowfall over the Park Range on Friday into Saturday. Confidence is still low on how much snow will fall as some details remain uncertain. This is especially true if strong northwest flow sets up further north. If you are planning on traveling during this time, be prepared for the possibility of difficult travel conditions, especially over the northern Colorado mountains. There is also a possibility of impacts south of the Park Range but confidence remains low on the exact details. After Friday and Saturday, guidance becomes more uncertain with multiple different scenarios. There is potential for the pattern to remain active into Sunday and early next week.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Transitory ridging builds across the region into Wednesday, leading to dry conditions and warming temperatures, with latest operational and ensemble model continuing to indicate eastern Pacific energy splitting as it translates across the Intermountain West Thursday and Friday, keeping the region in moderate northwest flow into the end of the Thanksgiving Holiday weekend.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Trending warmer and drier into the Thanksgiving Holiday Weekend.

sections.name: Update
paragraphs: Updated to bring down the Winter Weather Advisories there were in effect for portions of the area this evening. Radar, area webcams and observations indicate snow is winding down, and will continue to do so through 10 PM. Little if any additional accumulations are expected across the higher terrain, and a rain-snow mix will remain possible along the southern I-25 corridor.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Current water vapor imagery and upper air analysis has increasing southwest flow aloft across the region as a broad upper trough continues to dig across the Great Basin. Regional radars increasing echoes along and west of the Continental Divide, with some echoes also developing across the higher terrain the Sangres at this time. Partly to mostly cloudy skies have helped to kept temperatures on the cool side, with readings in the 40s across the plains and mainly in the 20s and 30s across the higher terrain at this time.

Current model data remains in good agreement of said upper trough digging into the Four Corners region through the late afternoon, and then lifting out across the Rockies through the overnight hours and into the High Plains into Tuesday morning. Steep lapse rates, along with increased uvv associated with a couple jet core lifting out across south central and southeast Colorado will bring bands of moderate to heavy snowfall into the Continental Divide this afternoon, with the bands continuing to lift out across the higher terrain into the southeast plains through the evening and into the over night hours. Higher impacts from these bands of snow, with quick bursts of 1 to 2 inches per hour possible, have prompted short fused Winter Weather Advisories (based on possible impacts and not total snow amounts) across the Continental Divide, as well as the Sangre de Cristo mountains into the southern I-25 Corridor with the potential for additional snow squall warnings being issued through the evening. Some higher res model data also indicate to potential for bursts heavy snow across portions of the San Luis Valley, the Wet Mtn Valley and across portions of the the Lower Arkansas River Valley, in which we will continue to monitor for possible additions to Winter Weather highlights as well possible snow squall warnings.

Precipitation and clouds diminish from west to east through the overnight hours into Tuesday morning, save for a few possible snow showers across the Central mountains, as drier and subsident northwest flow takes hold across the Rockies. Temperatures to remain below seasonal levels mainly in the 40s across the plains, and 30s and 40s across the higher terrain, save for 20s at the peaks.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Transitory ridging builds across the region into Wednesday, leading to dry conditions and warming temperatures, with latest operational and ensemble model continuing to indicate eastern Pacific energy splitting as it translates across the Intermountain West Thursday and Friday, keeping the region in moderate northwest flow into the end of the Thanksgiving Holiday weekend. This will keep chances of precipitation confined mainly to the Northern and Central Mtns, with temperatures remaining at and above seasonal levels. However, will need to continue to monitor the potential for surface high pressure building across the Northern High Plains to send a backdoor cold front into eastern Colorado later next weekend.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: Confidence remains fairly high in a transition to a more progressive and active pattern next week.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - High pressure will bring dry weather and near-seasonal temperatures across the area through Thanksgiving.
- A more mild airmass will spread across the region for the upcoming weekend, boosting temperatures 5 to 10 degrees above normal for late November.
- A weather system brushing by northern Utah late Friday will bring a chance of valley rain/mountain snow mainly north of I-80.

- A more active weather pattern will return next week as a series of weather systems pass through the region. This far out, considerable uncertainty remains regarding the timing and track of these systems.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Mid level ridging building into the Great Basin this evening will become the dominant weather feature through Thanksgiving. With this ridge in place, warmer temperatures aloft and light winds will result likely allow valley inversions to become established through Thanksgiving, which may allow for patchy early morning stratus/fog. A weak weather system fighting through this ridge will be splitting as it moves inland, bringing little more than an increase in cloud cover Wednesday. Low elevation temperatures will remain near to perhaps slightly above climo through Thanksgiving, while higher elevations see a warming trend.

Late Friday into Saturday, a more robust shortwave will crest the Great Basin ridge, and guidance has been shifting toward a more amplified solution digging this wave through the central Rockies, and pushing a cold front through the Forecast area. Roughly 60% of ensemble solutions (heavily influenced by EC members) now spread precipitation into northern Utah Friday night into early Saturday as this front pushes through the region.

Confidence remains fairly high in a transition to a more progressive and active pattern next week. Timing and track of individual waves and the associated chance for precipitation remains uncertain as would be expected this far out, but ensemble families are in good agreement developing negative height anomalies during the first half of next week.

2660.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Brian Lazar
bottom_line: You can trigger an avalanche large enough to bury you on slopes steeper than about 30 degrees at higher elevations. The most dangerous slopes are those with wind-drifted snow that face west to north through east. If you experience audible collapsing or shooting cracks, give suspect slopes a wide buffer and stick to lower-angle terrain, as you can trigger avalanches from a distance or from below.
Slopes less than 30 degrees in wind-sheltered areas and slopes below treeline offer safer travel options.

2753.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Kreston Rohrig
bottom_line: There's still a good chance you can trigger an avalanche on steep wind-drifted slopes facing northwest to north to east as you approach or enter the alpine. Fresh slabs formed over the weekend rest on well-connected weak layers in deeper areas and can fail from a distance away. By sticking to lower-angle, sheltered slopes, or more southerly aspects, you will lessen your odds of triggering a slide.

2754.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Brian Lazar
bottom_line: Most slopes are generally safe from avalanches due to shallow or discontinuous snow cover. You might be able to trigger a small avalanche where recent winds have formed pockets of stiffened snow below ridgelines, on lee slopes, and around rocky outcrops in the alpine.

2745.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Andrew McWilliams
bottom_line: Snow cover is still too thin for avalanches on most slopes. In the alpine, you should steer around hard drifts of snow on steep terrain features and below ridgetops. Unfortunately, the slopes with enough snow to ride are also where you might find enough snow for slides.

3046.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

1736.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

3014.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
bottom_line: Elevations above 7,000 feet have 1-2 feet of snow on the ground. You may encounter pockets of wind slabs above 7,500 feet on north- and east-facing terrain. If the snow feels stiff or slabby underfoot, then find a different aspect away from wind-drifted snow. The biggest hazard remains thin snow cover and hitting rocks, logs, and stumps. Even a small slide through thin coverage could end a season before it even starts.
We'll update the General Avalanche Information weekly until full-time forecasting operations begin.
hazard_discussion: Above 7,000 feet, a layered snowpack is beginning to build for the season. Good, albeit thin, skiing and riding conditions have been reported at upper elevations. Elevations below 7,000 feet remain thin and bony. Before November 13th, most slopes were bare. Winter trailhead access remains a challenge as there is not quite enough snow to launch sleds. Most forest roads become impassable by vehicle above 6,500 feet. As folks start poking around the mountains, remember that avalanches can occur with just a few feet of snow on the ground. There may be some lingering pockets of wind slabs above 7,500 feet on north and east-facing terrain features, particularly just below ridgelines.

Beginning Thanksgiving Day, a large storm system will impact the Pacific and Interior Northwest. Strong winds, mountain snow, and fluctuating rain/snow levels will be in the cards for several days. Pay attention to changing weather and snow conditions heading into the weekend. Stay up to date on mountain weather with our WEATHER tab, where you'll find webcams, weather stations, and weather forecasting tools.

Fresh wind slabs will come back onto the menu with more snow and wind later this week. Pay attention to gullies that can become crossloaded and may also act as a terrain trap. Look for clues of wind-affected snow, such as drifts, dunes, pillows, and freshly built cornices. Watch for signs of instability, such as shooting cracks. If you're observing these signs, find another aspect away from wind-drifted snow.
Turn On Your Snow and Avalanche Brain

• Beacons, shovels, probes, airbags. Run through all your gear and make sure it's functioning properly. Does your transceiver or airbag need any firmware updates? Look for cracks, defects, or corroded batteries. Make it fun with your friends and do a pre-season gear check with your winter travel companions.
• Check out the Education tab on our website to sign up for avalanche courses this winter (COURSES ).

• Help us paint a picture of what's going on in the mountains. If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation HERE. A simple photo and/or weather observation helps forecasters and the public alike.

2755.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Andrew McWilliams
bottom_line: The snow cover is too thin for slides on most slopes, so avalanche danger is LOW. Recent snow drifts rest on weak, old snow. If you find a continuous drift of firm snow on a steep terrain feature, you can trigger a small slide. Steer around drifted pockets of snow where you see them below ridges or inside gullies.
